source: Klein G, Klinger D (1991) Naturalistic decision making. Human Systems IAC Gateway 2(1)
finding: Klein's own early account of how the model arose. Researchers watched urban fireground commanders (FGCs) handle non-routine fires. The commanders said they were not making choices, considering alternatives or assessing probabilities. The team found no evidence for extensive option generation and could see no way to apply optimal choice.
numbers: No counts given in this short article (no N, no percent of decisions).
quote: We found no evidence for extensive option generation. Rarely were even two options concurrently evaluated.
limits: Short magazine-style summary. The numbers sit in the 1986 and 1988 reports, which could not be opened (DTIC blocked).
agent_relevance: Origin claim for S0/S3: the first option comes from situation recognition, not from a list. Fits our rule that the program, not a comparison step, should drive early choice.

source: Klein G, Klinger D (1991) Naturalistic decision making. Human Systems IAC Gateway 2(1)
finding: Three RPD cases. (A) Simple match: situation recognised, the typical action is carried out. (B) Developing a course of action: the person consciously evaluates the action, usually with imagery, to find problems before acting. (C) Complex case: evaluation finds flaws, the action is modified, or rejected and the next most typical action is tried. Recognition brings four things: plausible goals, critical cues, expectancies, typical actions.
numbers: Three variants; four recognition products (goals, cues, expectancies, action).
quote: the evaluation reveals flaws requiring modification, or the option is judged inadequate and rejected in favor of the next most typical reaction
limits: Boxes-and-arrows model. It does not say how typicality is computed or how many options are tried before giving up.
agent_relevance: Direct template for a loop: propose first typical option, simulate it, on a flaw repair or move to next typical option. Maps to S3 then a check state.

source: Klein G, Klinger D (1991) Naturalistic decision making. Human Systems IAC Gateway 2(1)
finding: Klein lists seven key features of RPD: first option is usually workable, not random generation and selective retention; serial not concurrent evaluation; satisficing not optimising; evaluation by mental simulation; focus on elaborating options not choosing between them; focus on situation assessment not decision events; decision maker primed to act.
numbers: 7 features in Table 2.
quote: RPDs are marked by an absence of comparison among options.
limits: Claimed as a model of experienced people, not novices. The article says it is not an alternative to analytic methods but sits on one continuum with them.
agent_relevance: Feature 5 (improve one option rather than choose among many) is the key contrast with best-of-N. For an LLM the equivalent is repair of one candidate.

source: Klein G, Klinger D (1991) Naturalistic decision making. Human Systems IAC Gateway 2(1)
finding: Tests of the model in other domains were reported as good support: fireground command, battle planning, critical care nursing, corporate information management, chess tournament play. Coding was evaluated at 87 to 94 percent inter-rater reliability. A 1989 Dayton workshop gathered 31 professionals from military, NASA, firms and universities.
numbers: Inter-rater reliability 87-94%; 31 workshop attendees.
limits: Reliability is of the coding of interviews. It says nothing about whether the model predicts choices. Evidence is from interviews, not experiments.
agent_relevance: Shows what evidence the model rests on: coded interview accounts. Treat claimed frequencies as [S] single-tradition evidence.

source: Klein G, Klinger D (1991) Naturalistic decision making. Human Systems IAC Gateway 2(1)
finding: Klein places recognitional and analytical strategies at opposite ends of one continuum, similar to Hammond's cognitive continuum. Under time pressure the decision maker is poised to act while evaluating a promising option, instead of waiting for an evaluation of several. Classical methods were mostly tested on students (inexperienced subjects).
numbers: n/a
limits: Claims about analytic methods failing under time pressure are argued, not tested in this text.
agent_relevance: Supports a budget-driven choice: cheap recognitional path first, analytic path only when a signal says so (guardrail G1).

source: Klein G, Wright C (2016) Macrocognition: from theory to toolbox. Frontiers in Psychology 7:54
finding: Klein states that RPD accounted for 80 to 90 percent of firefighter decisions, and that the model needed 10 to 20 years of experience so could not have been found in the lab. He lists replications: military leaders (Schmitt and Klein 1999), firefighters (Keren et al 2013), offshore oil platform managers (Skriver 1998). Tests of the model itself: Klein et al 1995 (chess), Johnson and Raab 2003 (handball).
numbers: 80-90% of fireground decisions; 10-20 years experience; 3 named replications; 2 named direct tests.
limits: Written by the model's author, a perspective piece. Percent is given without N. The 80-90% here is higher than the 80% (prototype match) and 12% (comparison) usually quoted from the 1986 study. Schmitt and Klein is not independent of Klein's circle.
agent_relevance: Frequency claims differ by source (80%, 80-90%, 46-96%). Do not wire any single percent into the agent; make the match-vs-compare split a measured quantity.

source: Klein G, Wright C (2016) Macrocognition: from theory to toolbox. Frontiers in Psychology 7:54
finding: History of the field. NDM was catalysed by Judith Orasanu's Army Research Institute program; about 30 researchers met in 1989 and the book Decision Making in Action (1993) followed. In 2001 Lipshitz et al in JBDM drew 16 commentaries, centred on the view that NDM needed more rigorous controlled methods. Klein replies that controlled studies would remove the expertise that makes the effect appear.
numbers: ~30 researchers in 1989; 16 commentaries on Lipshitz et al 2001; 12 NDM conferences by 2016.
limits: Author is a participant. Reply about lab studies is an argument, not a result.
agent_relevance: Explains why quantitative evidence is thin: our own agent tests (bench harness) can supply the controlled comparison the field lacks.

source: Klein G (2021) The RPD model: criticisms and confusions. Psychology Today
finding: Klein answers six criticisms. He says RPD has two parts: fast pattern matching and slower mental simulation, and maps them to System 1 and System 2. He says simple computer versions leave out simulation. He says the model first looked like a time-pressure model but also appears under slow conditions. Inexperienced people use the RPD tactic less than half the time.
numbers: Novices use RPD under 50% of the time (no N given). Chess study cited: Klein et al 1995.
quote: the first option the skilled chess players consider is of high quality
limits: Blog post. No sample sizes, effect sizes or statistics. Critics are not named.
agent_relevance: Klein himself says a recognition-only implementation is incomplete. Our agent needs both the first-guess step and a separate simulation or check step with its own state.

source: Klein G (2021) The RPD model: criticisms and confusions. Psychology Today
finding: Falsifiability argument. If skilled people generate options at random, the model fails. In the 1995 chess study the first option skilled players considered was of high quality, so the model survived the test. Klein says the evidence base is thin because it comes from field studies, and defends them as the only way to see the effect of 10 to 20 years of experience.
numbers: Chess test: first-move quality high (no figures on the page).
limits: The page gives no figures for the chess test. A later study (Moxley 2012, see another line) finds that the first move is often not the final move.
agent_relevance: A useful falsification test for our agent: is the first sample from the model better than a random sample from its own distribution? Measure it rather than assume.

source: Ambur O (2004) Recognition-primed decision-making: implications for record-keeping (a page-cited digest of Klein 1998 Sources of Power)
finding: Klein's singular versus comparative evaluation. Singular evaluation means judging each option on its own merits, even if you cycle through several. He ties it to Simon's satisficing. The second puzzle was how the options get evaluated; his answer was mental simulation, which he says is not foolproof but usually better than anything else the commanders could do.
numbers: Page refs in Sources of Power: pp. 17, 20-21, 24.
quote: the way they evaluate that course of action by imagining it
limits: Secondary digest of the book by a records-management writer. Quotes carry page numbers but were not checked against the book.
agent_relevance: Defines the two engine parts for our schema: a satisficing generator (one option at a time) and a simulation check. Neither needs a score table.

source: Ambur O (2004) Recognition-primed decision-making: implications for record-keeping (a page-cited digest of Klein 1998 Sources of Power)
finding: Limits on mental simulation as Klein reports them. Simulations used few parts, generally no more than three, and about six transitions. He ties this to working memory. Chunking from familiarity lets people stretch it.
numbers: Max about 3 moving parts; about 6 transition steps (Sources of Power p. 52).
quote: a maximum of three moving parts
limits: Derived from interviews and Klein's own reading of them; no controlled capacity test is reported in this digest. LLM context limits differ from human working memory.
agent_relevance: Design rule for the check step: keep a simulated walk-through short (about 6 steps, few variables). Long chains accumulate error; split them.

source: Ambur O (2004) Recognition-primed decision-making: implications for record-keeping (a page-cited digest of Klein 1998 Sources of Power)
finding: Weaknesses of mental simulation named by Klein. People fall in love with the simulation they built. They explain away contradicting evidence (de minimis explanations). Marvin Cohen's snap-back idea: people keep patching one simulation until the patches pile up, then go looking for an alternative. Simulation produces explanations, not proofs.
numbers: Sources of Power pp. 68-69, 72.
quote: once we have built a mental simulation, we tend to fall in love with it
limits: Cohen's snap-back is a hypothesis in this text, not a measured result here.
agent_relevance: Matches guardrails G2 and G3: a simulation by the same model that wrote the plan is a weak check. Require the walk-through to cite concrete outputs and trigger an alternative when the patch count passes a limit.

source: Ambur O (2004) Recognition-primed decision-making: implications for record-keeping (a page-cited digest of Klein 1998 Sources of Power)
finding: Frequency of recognitional strategy across Klein's studies was large, between 46 percent and 96 percent, with little evidence of comparative evaluation. Klein says people compare options more with unfamiliar situations, because inexperience limits generating reasonable options or confidence. He also states that RPD predominates even when time is enough for comparison.
numbers: 46% to 96% recognitional across studies (p. 99). No study-level breakdown in the digest.
limits: Range pooled across domains and across coders. The low end (46%) is not tied to a named study here. 'Predominates even when time is sufficient' is asserted.
agent_relevance: The spread is large, so the mix of match vs compare depends on domain familiarity. Our agent should estimate familiarity (does an exemplar match?) before choosing the path.

source: Ambur O (2004) Recognition-primed decision-making: implications for record-keeping (a page-cited digest of Klein 1998 Sources of Power)
finding: Two often-mixed 80 percent claims. One: fireground commanders make about 80 percent of their decisions in under a minute (Sources of Power, quoted by the digest). Two: in the 1986 study about 80 percent of decision points were prototype matches (see the unopened 1986 line). Also Klein's expectancy safeguard: if the reading is right, expectancies match events; if wrong, anomalies get noticed.
numbers: 80% of decisions in under 1 minute (Klein p. 4 as quoted).
quote: rely on their expectancies as one safeguard
limits: Time claim is not a measured result in the digest. Expectancy check is a claim from interviews.
agent_relevance: The expectancy idea is a concrete check: before acting, write what you expect to see next; if reality differs, reopen the diagnosis. Cheap and code-checkable.

source: Klein G, Calderwood R, Clinton-Cirocco A (1986) Rapid decision making on the fire ground. Proc Human Factors Society 30th Annual Meeting 1:576-580 (extended in ARI Technical Report 796, 1988)
finding: The founding fireground study, as reported by secondary summaries seen in search results only: 26 experienced commanders, 156 decision points probed. Over 80 percent were handled by matching the situation to a typical prototype and acting. Under 12 percent showed any simultaneous comparison of two or more options.
numbers: 26 FGCs (mean experience 23 years); 156 decision points; >80% prototype match; <12% comparison. Taken from search summaries, not from the report.
limits: Not opened: the DTIC link returned a bot-check page. Retrospective interviews, critical-incident method, selected non-routine incidents, no control group, coder was a member of the research team.
agent_relevance: Do not treat these as verified. The agent design should rest on the mechanism, not on the exact 80 and 12.

source: Kaempf GL, Klein G, Thordsen ML, Wolf S (1996) Decision making in complex naval command-and-control environments. Human Factors 38(2):220-231
finding: RPD tested with AEGIS cruiser air-warfare officers. Search results confirm the citation but the findings were not retrieved. A different report (Kaempf, Wolf, Miller 1993, quoted in a Navy report) found 87 percent of situation-assessment information transactions were feature matching, and command-level officers picked actions almost only by recognising applicable tactics.
numbers: 87% feature matching (1993 report, via a secondary snippet). The 1996 paper's own recognitional percentage was not verified.
limits: Not opened. Do not cite a percentage for the 1996 paper from this line.
agent_relevance: A second high-stakes team setting with the same mechanism. Open the paper before using any figure.

source: Johnson JG, Raab M (2003) Take the first: option-generation and resulting choices. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 91(2):215-229
finding: The main controlled test of the first-option claim, seen through a summary page. 85 young male handball players watched 31 frozen game scenes, said their first option, then generated more options and chose. Option quality, rated by four coaches, fell with each new option. Using only the first option would on average have given better choices. Players more often changed a good first choice to a poor final one than a poor first to a good one.
numbers: N=85 (German and Brazilian, ages 13-18, 6-11 years experience); 31 scenes; 4.23 options per scene; 107 distinct solutions rated by 4 coaches on a 5-level scale.
limits: Read through a blog summary, not the paper (paywalled). Participants were youth players, not elite experts. Ratings by coaches, not outcomes. The authors say the strategy needs familiar, ill-defined tasks with repeated exposure and feedback.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence that more options can hurt. Warns against generate-then-pick: a second-guessing step that replaces a good first answer. Supports G1 (doubt only on a signal).

source: Bossard C, Kerivel T, Dugeny S, Bagot P, Fontaine T, Kermarrec G (2022) Naturalistic decision-making in sport: how current advances into the Recognition Primed Decision model offer insights for future research. Frontiers in Psychology 13:936140
finding: Citing Macquet's 2020 review of RPD in sport: 60 to 81 percent of expert decisions were simple matches, 13 to 28 percent diagnosis, 3 to 24 percent evaluation of a course of action. Athletes far from the ball had more time for mental simulation. Rugby coaches, under less time pressure, used deliberative decisions often. Athletes chose their preferred first option in about 80 percent of decisions.
numbers: Simple match 60-81%; diagnose 13-28%; evaluate 3-24% (Macquet 2020 review); first option chosen about 80%.
limits: Opinion paper summarising a review. The authors say consistent evidence for an intuitive-to-analytic continuum in sport is lacking. Mostly qualitative studies.
agent_relevance: The evaluate-by-simulation level is the rarest (3-24%). Simulation is a fallback, used when a signal says the match is unsafe.

source: Bossard et al (2022), same paper, section on creativity
finding: A link between first-option quality and creativity: Klatt et al (2019) found, with coaches and soccer players watching real match video, a positive correlation between a player's creativity score and the quality of the first option they generated. The paper also notes that choosing the first option 80 percent of the time could look non-creative.
numbers: Two studies (coaches; soccer players) per Klatt 2019; no r value given here.
limits: Second-hand, no effect sizes. Relation between intuition and creativity is not established in sport science.
agent_relevance: Bridge to the creativity subfields: recognition gives workable options, not novel ones. A novelty step must be added separately and judged by running (G8).

source: Intuition and deliberation in elite expertise (2026) Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications (journal not confirmed; authors not captured, initials MV and PT), introduction reviewing Calderwood, Klein and Crandall 1988; Gobet and Simon 1996; Chabris and Hearst 2003
finding: Review of chess time-pressure studies. Calderwood, Klein and Crandall (1988) compared three class B players with three masters in blitz and slower games. The weaker players did worse in blitz; the masters seemed immune, which was read as evidence for intuition. The authors point out the tiny sample. Gobet and Simon's result on Kasparov in simultaneous play was challenged: his rating dropped from 2750 to 2646, which would put him near 60th. Chabris and Hearst found grandmasters (Elo 2530 to 2790) made more and larger blunders in 15-minute rapid games than in standard games.
numbers: Calderwood 1988: 3 vs 3 players. Kasparov Elo 2750 to 2646. Chabris and Hearst 2003: GM Elo 2530-2790. Burns 2004: blitz ranks explain 64-81% of variance in standard ratings.
limits: Review by authors who argue against the intuition account. 'Immune to time pressure' rested on very small N.
agent_relevance: The chess evidence that is often used for RPD is weaker than usually told. Expect some loss when thinking budget is cut, even for strong players.

source: Intuition and deliberation in elite expertise (2026) Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications (journal not confirmed; authors not captured, initials MV and PT), reporting Moxley, Ericsson, Charness, Krampe (2012)
finding: Contrary test of the take-first view in chess (Moxley et al 2012, as described). Players found the best move in tactical positions with verbal protocols, 5 minutes each. Stronger players (mean Elo 2194) beat weaker (1836). Final moves were better than the first move mentioned, mainly in hard positions. Players kept the first move as final only 45 percent of the time overall.
numbers: Elo 2194 vs 1836; first move kept 45% overall; hard positions 22% (stronger) and 25% (weaker); easy positions 73% (stronger) and 50% (weaker).
limits: Second-hand description. Players had 5 minutes, so it is not a time-pressure design. Positions were tactical puzzles, not natural games.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: first-option value depends on difficulty. Easy items keep the first answer; hard ones need search. A difficulty signal should gate the extra deliberation.

source: Intuition and deliberation in elite expertise (2026) Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications (journal not confirmed; authors not captured, initials MV and PT), Study 1
finding: Study 1: 20 grandmasters at Wijk aan Zee in 1998 and 1999 played standard games (about 3 min per move) and blitz (about 7.5 s per move). Computer-judged blunders per move nearly doubled in blitz. 18 of 20 players had a higher blunder rate in blitz.
numbers: N=20 players, Elo 2540-2812 (mean 2671); t(19)=-5.79, p<.001, Cohen's d=1.30; 18 of 20 worse in blitz.
quote: performance of even experts of the highest skill level suffered when denied sufficient time to deliberate
limits: Within-subject but non-randomised; blitz and standard events are different tournaments. Computer judge counts all blunders. Authors argue against the RPD emphasis.
agent_relevance: Cutting thinking time hurts even experts. A recognition-only fast path is not free; keep a deliberate path available when a signal fires.

source: Intuition and deliberation in elite expertise (2026) Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications (journal not confirmed; authors not captured, initials MV and PT), Study 2
finding: Study 2: seven world chess champions in championship matches. Fast moves under 1 minute had fewer but bigger blunders. Fast moves made with under 5 minutes left had a higher blunder rate than fast moves with ample time. Elite players used time adaptively: quick when positions allowed it, slow when needed.
numbers: Move counts by time band: 2934 (fast), 2905, 2859, 2849, 1250 (10+ min). Threshold 5 minutes remaining.
limits: Archival data; time per move partly reflects position difficulty, which the authors note. Move times are integer minutes.
agent_relevance: Supports a learned or coded switch between quick and slow modes, as RPD itself implies (simple match vs evaluate). The mode choice is where skill shows.

source: Kahneman D, Klein G (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree. American Psychologist 64(6):515-526
finding: Joint paper by the two rival traditions (heuristics and biases; NDM). They agree that intuition quality depends on how predictable the environment is and on whether the person had a chance to learn its regularities. Subjective confidence is not a reliable sign of accuracy.
numbers: No new data; a position paper.
limits: Only the abstract was read (from Europe PMC). Full text was not available to open.
agent_relevance: The condition for trusting a recognitional first answer is validity of the environment plus practice. For the agent: trust the first answer only where cheap checks have shown past answers to be right (G3). Do not read confidence as evidence.

source: Cognitive task analysis to evaluate resident physician decision making in the ICU, critical decision method with RPD template (2025). Authors not captured
finding: RPD used as a coding frame for interviews with third-year medicine residents about fluid decisions in septic shock. Residents leaned on volume rules (about 3 to 5 litres) and on salient analogues. Premature closure, confirmation bias and status-quo bias were found. Residents rarely sought confirming or refuting information or considered other diagnoses after deciding.
numbers: 11 of 23 eligible residents interviewed; median 7 days from event to interview; 7 domains found (4 from RPD, 3 emerged).
limits: Small, single site, retrospective interviews, trainees not experts. Findings are about heuristics, not a test of the RPD mechanism.
agent_relevance: Failure case: first workable option plus no real check gives premature closure. The simulation step must be a real check against outside facts (G2, G3), not a restatement.

source: Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning (2026) JMIR Biomedical Engineering. Authors not captured
finding: Prompts told the model to reason by recognition-primed decision making, or by data-frame theory, and were compared with a plain prompt on 45 patient vignettes (emergency, non-emergency, self-care). Both raised accuracy. Gains were biggest for self-care advice, where the plain prompt almost never gave it. Gains were bigger for reasoning models than non-reasoning models.
numbers: 10 ChatGPT models x 45 vignettes x 3 prompts x 10 runs = 13,500 assessments. Accuracy: plain 63.3% (95% CI 61.9-64.7), RPD prompt 67.6% (66.3-69), data-frame 66.7% (65.3-68). OR 2.26 (RPD) and 2.05 (data-frame), both p<.001. Self-care accuracy 13.4% to 29.8% (RPD) and 24.6% (data-frame). Largest model gain: GPT-4.1 mini +13 points with the data-frame prompt.
limits: One domain, one benchmark. No matched-token control, so the gain may come from extra reasoning text, not from RPD content. Only 2 emergency and 30 non-emergency cases among 45, and performance on those was already high. Small absolute gain (about 4 points).
agent_relevance: Only direct LLM test of an RPD prompt so far. Gain is modest and the control is weak; per G7 we must rerun it at equal tokens before using it.

source: Hybrid BDI / Markov-logic implementation of the recognition-primed decision model (2019) Human-centric Computing and Information Sciences. Authors not captured
finding: A formal build of RPD as an agent. Situation recognition = Markov logic network trained on experience (an Experiential-Learning and Decision-Support module). Diagnosis of untypical cases = ontology-based feature matching. Mental simulation = Bayesian network giving the probability of an effect given a cause. The authors say earlier RPD implementations were more descriptive than formal.
numbers: Trained on 80% and tested on 20% of data for FIRE and EVACUATE situations; compared with a human training study of 36 participants (groups of 17 and 19; group 1 used for comparison).
limits: One small evacuation case study. Validation compares agent output with human data, not with a baseline agent. Mental simulation as a Bayesian network is a modelling choice, not Klein's account.
agent_relevance: Shows the three RPD parts can be separate modules with different machinery. For an LLM agent: recognise (retrieval/classify), diagnose (feature matching), simulate (separate check) as code-driven states.

source: Warwick, McIlwaine, Hutton, McDermott (2001); Stanard et al (2001); Lebiere, Gonzalez, Warwick (2009); Sokolowski (2003) computational RPD models, as seen in search results
finding: Earlier computational RPD models, known only from search summaries. Warwick and colleagues built RPDm on Hintzman's multiple-trace memory (MINERVA 2), with a driver agent at a traffic light seeded from a cognitive task analysis of six drivers. Lebiere, Gonzalez and Warwick compared RPD-based and ACT-R instance-based learning models: both satisfactory but not human-like. Sokolowski's RPDAgent claims decisions equivalent to humans (self-report).
numbers: 6 drivers in the task analysis. No performance numbers retrieved.
limits: Not opened. Paper links failed (bot checks, 404). Do not rely on any claim here.
agent_relevance: RPD-as-memory-retrieval (similarity to past traces) is the formal core. Matches our idea of retrieving past solved cases (see analogical access subfield).

source: Carrigan S (undated, likely 2016-2018) Fireground decision-making: a qualitative study. New Hampshire Fire Academy applied research paper hosted by USFA
finding: Small replication-style test: four shift commanders from one New Hampshire department watched fire videos and gave plausible goals, cues, expectancies and actions. The author reports support for the RPD model and a high level of consistency between participants.
numbers: N=4 shift commanders (all four shifts of the department), each with 20+ years experience; videos of real fires.
limits: Student applied-research paper, not peer reviewed. N=4. Video size-up is not real command. Year is a guess (not read on the page). Confirms the coding categories, not the 80% claim.
agent_relevance: Weak. Included only as an example of the replication strength actually available outside Klein's group.

source: Time spent thinking in online chess reflects the value of computation (2025) PMC12553403. Authors not captured
finding: Over 12 million online chess games, players spent more time thinking in positions where extra computation would help more, and this was stronger in stronger players. A simple cost model captured the pattern. Read from the abstract only.
numbers: More than 12 million games.
limits: Abstract only. Observational data from online play.
agent_relevance: Evidence that skilled players switch between fast and slow thinking by value of thought. Supports gating extra deliberation on a signal (see Resource-rational analysis subfield).

source: Assessing military professionals' endorsement of decision-making assumptions: an exploratory factor analysis (2026) PMC13113691. Authors not captured
finding: Survey on how far Norwegian military professionals endorse Klein's 11 decision-making claims. Endorsement is not one factor: two factors fitted better, Planning/Structure and Analytic/Evidence-based practices.
numbers: N=225 active-duty personnel; KMO=0.741; two factors explain 29.24% of variance; alpha 0.65 and about 0.71.
limits: Abstract only. Measures beliefs, not decisions.
agent_relevance: Low. Shows even practitioners hold both views: structure and recognition. No design implication beyond mixing both.

source: Klein GA (1993) A recognition-primed decision (RPD) model of rapid decision making. In Klein, Orasanu, Calderwood, Zsambok (eds) Decision Making in Action: Models and Methods. Ablex, ch. 6, pp. 138-147
finding: The full statement of the model. Situation assessment generates one plausible course of action; mental simulation evaluates it. The fireground commanders (FGCs) said they were not making choices or comparing options. Klein admits he cannot show they were not comparing unconsciously, and says the burden of proof lies on those who claim hidden comparison. His reasons: analytic strategies are unlikely in under a minute, each FGC denied comparing, and they described a different strategy.
numbers: No new counts in this passage. Funded by US Army Research Institute contracts (numbers garbled in OCR).
quote: We have no way of demonstrating that the fireground commanders weren't contrasting alternative options, but the burden of proof is not on us.
limits: The central claim rests on commanders' retrospective reports. Klein himself says it cannot be disproved that they compared options below awareness. Lipshitz (same book) argues for a definition that avoids this.
agent_relevance: Honest limit for our own design: a model's written reasoning is also a retrospective story. We should use behaviour (which candidate was tried first, what was changed) rather than the model's account of its process.

source: Klein GA (1993) A recognition-primed decision (RPD) model of rapid decision making. In Klein, Orasanu, Calderwood, Zsambok (eds) Decision Making in Action: Models and Methods. Ablex, ch. 6, pp. 138-147, Table 6.1
finding: Klein tabulated how often RPD strategies were used rather than concurrent comparison of options for non-routine decisions across five studies. Coding was liberal toward analytic: any sign that two or more options were contrasted counted as analytic. Recognitional use was 80 percent for urban FGCs (all decision points including trivial ones), 58 percent for expert FGCs and 46 percent for novice FGCs on the hard command points, 51 percent for wildfire incident commanders, under 50 percent (42 percent) for tank platoon cadets, 60 percent for experienced design engineers not under time pressure.
numbers: FGC-1: 156 decision points, 80% (mean 23 years experience). FGC-2: experts 48 points 58%; novices 33 points 46%. Wildfire: 110 points, 51% (56% functional decisions, 39% organisational; commanders mean 24 years). Tank platoon: 55 points, 42% (cadets in first 10 days). Design engineers: 51 points, 60%. Intercoder agreement 87-94% (Taynor, Crandall, Wiggins 1987). Table read from OCR; point counts matched to rows by order.
limits: Only the first row supports the oft-quoted 80 percent; it includes trivial decisions. When only hard command decisions were counted, experts fell to 58 percent. Counts are decision points, not people. Coders belong to the research group. No control for outcome quality.
agent_relevance: Strong correction of the headline: 80 percent is the top of a 42 to 80 percent range, and experience raised the rate only 12 points (58 vs 46). Treat recognition-first as the common path, not the only one. Plan for 40 to 60 percent of hard cases needing comparison.

source: Klein GA (1993) A recognition-primed decision (RPD) model of rapid decision making. In Klein, Orasanu, Calderwood, Zsambok (eds) Decision Making in Action: Models and Methods. Ablex, ch. 6, pp. 138-147, conditions and dangers
finding: Klein's boundary conditions. Recognition is more likely when the person is experienced, time pressure is greater and conditions are less stable. Analysis prevails when data are abstract and alphanumeric rather than perceptual, when problems are very combinatorial, when constituencies disagree, and when the choice must be justified. Dangers of misusing recognition: lacking the experience to produce a good first option, being unable to simulate and see pitfalls, or failing to optimise when needed. For predicting an enemy's plan, recognition can give tunnel vision and self-deception.
numbers: n/a (stated conclusions)
quote: the danger of misapplying recognitional decision strategies is that personnel will lack the experience needed
limits: Conditions are Klein's summary of his own studies plus Hammond's work; not from a single controlled comparison.
agent_relevance: Gives a rule list for when the fast path is unsafe: abstract symbolic data, combinatorial search, adversarial settings, need to justify. Puzzle and ARC-type tasks with combinatorial structure sit on the analytic side.

source: Klein GA (1993) A recognition-primed decision (RPD) model of rapid decision making. In Klein, Orasanu, Calderwood, Zsambok (eds) Decision Making in Action: Models and Methods. Ablex, ch. 6, pp. 138-147, footnote 1
finding: Negative result worth keeping. Klein's team expected commanders to retrieve past cases (analogues). Despite probes, commanders rarely identified analogues they used. No past incident matched a whole new one. Analogues were cited as helpful only for parts of an incident. Klein reads this as experience being merged into a judgement of familiarity or prototypicality, not retrieval of single cases.
numbers: No counts given.
quote: the fireground commanders rarely were able to identify analogues they had used
limits: Based on the commanders' ability to report. Recall of individual cases may still occur without report.
agent_relevance: Informs the link to the analogical-access subfield: do not assume recognition equals case retrieval. A prototype or schema summary may be the better store than raw past cases.

source: Klein GA (1993) A recognition-primed decision (RPD) model of rapid decision making. In Klein, Orasanu, Calderwood, Zsambok (eds) Decision Making in Action: Models and Methods. Ablex, ch. 6, pp. 138-147, worked examples
finding: Three worked cases. (1) Laundry-chute fire: first read was a vertical shaft fire, the action was to send hose teams up; expectancies failed when crews reported they were too late; smoke under the eaves shifted the reading to a building-wide fire, and the action switched to search and rescue plus a second alarm. (2) Libyan airliner: the general simulated how an innocent pilot would act, could not build a plausible story, and used that failure as evidence of hostile intent. (3) Forest fire: a staff member simulated a wind shift that would bring fire across a key road; the prime option was rejected and replaced by a second one, with no comparison of the two roads.
numbers: Three cases; no counts.
limits: Chosen illustrations from interviews, not a sample. They show the mechanism but not how often it succeeds.
agent_relevance: Shows three uses of simulation: check a plan (road), test a reading by trying to build a story (airliner), and notice a broken expectancy that forces re-diagnosis (chute). Our check state can have all three.

source: Lipshitz R (1993) Converging themes in the study of decision making in realistic settings. In Klein et al (eds) Decision Making in Action. Ablex, ch. 5 (RPD summary at pp. 107-110; critique of the choice view at pp. 179-180)
finding: An independent restatement of RPD as three phases: situation recognition, serial option evaluation, mental simulation. Actions sit in a queue ordered by typicality, and the most typical one is tried first. Simulation has four outcomes: implement as is, modify, reject and take the next action, or reassess the situation because the imagined future exposed something unnoticed. Lipshitz says no step works without domain knowledge, and that expertise shows in finer distinctions, better analogies, richer imagined developments and faster rejection of bad actions, not in analytic skill.
numbers: Three phases; four simulation outcomes.
quote: The last step in the model, mental simulation, guards against the mistakes that result from uncritical thinking.
limits: A review by a sympathetic fellow researcher. The action queue ordered by typicality is Lipshitz's formalisation, not a measured structure.
agent_relevance: The queue-by-typicality plus four-outcome simulation is a ready state machine for S3 and the check state. The reassess outcome is the link back to diagnosis, and it is the signal-driven doubt that G1 allows.

source: Lipshitz R (1993), pp. 179-180 in Decision Making in Action: matching versus choice
finding: Objection and reply. If decisions are defined as choices, RPD can be read as a nondeliberate comparison among alternatives. Lipshitz says this is contrary to the essence of RPD, which is matching (action chosen from situation recognition) followed by reassessment (testing the chosen action by simulating its execution). He proposes that a decision be defined as an action argument ('do A because R') rather than a choice.
numbers: n/a
limits: A conceptual argument; no data. It answers a definition problem, not the empirical question of whether options are compared.
agent_relevance: For an LLM the matching/choice split is clean in code: either the program holds a list of scored candidates and picks (choice) or it holds one candidate and keeps or repairs it (matching). Log which one a run used.

source: Klein GA (1993) Twenty questions: suggestions for research in naturalistic decision making. In Decision Making in Action, pp. 393-395 read
finding: Klein's own list of open questions at the end of the founding book. Question 1: when is it better to compare options than to imagine a favourite option more clearly? Question 3: are an experienced person's first options more likely to succeed than later ones? He notes there had been little work on mental simulation; de Groot's progressive deepening is one exception; Kahneman and Tversky's simulation heuristic warns of recency, availability and anchoring errors that may also arise in field settings. He asks where the expectations that judge a simulated outcome come from.
numbers: 20 questions; those on first-option success and on simulation quoted above.
limits: Stated as research questions in 1993. Some were later partly answered (Johnson and Raab 2003 for question 3; Moxley 2012 gives a counter-case).
agent_relevance: These open questions are directly testable on an LLM: (3) is the first sample better than later ones, per difficulty; (1) compare repair-one-candidate against compare-many at equal tokens. Both fit our bench harness.

source: Orasanu J, Salas E (1993) Team decision making in complex environments, citing Klein and Thordsen (1989b), in Decision Making in Action
finding: Reported indirect support that teams follow the same strategy as individuals. Klein and Thordsen observed four types of teams (military command and control, crisis management, firefighting, cockpit crews). Rather than generating all options and comparing them at once, they classed the situation as a familiar type and retrieved the most plausible response.
numbers: 4 team types; no counts or team numbers given in the passage.
limits: Second-hand citation of an unpublished report; no data in the passage.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence that the pattern scales to groups. Relevant only to the multi-agent case, which we keep out of scope (SCHEMA 4b).
